title: Long-Distance Relationship Tips: How to Make It Work — cv.cm
description: How to make a long-distance relationship work: a plan to close the distance, how often to talk, time zones, date ideas, visits and signs it is not working.
h1: How do you make a long-distance relationship work?
answer: A long-distance relationship works best when both people share a plan to live in the same place one day, trust each other, and keep a simple routine of contact. Talk often enough to feel close, but focus on real conversation, not hours online. Plan visits ahead, say worries early and kindly, and check every few months that you still want the same future.

sections.h: What makes a long-distance relationship work
body: Long distance is common: students in different cities, jobs abroad, couples who met online in different countries. In Chinese it is 异地恋, in Japanese 遠距離恋愛, in Korean 장거리 연애, in Vietnamese yêu xa. The problems are similar everywhere: missing touch, time zones, the cost of travel, and the worry that the other person is drifting away.

Research gives some hope. A US study by Kelmer and colleagues found that people in long-distance relationships reported relationship quality as good as, or better than, people living close to their partner. But by the follow-up, they were just as likely to have broken up. Distance does not doom a couple, and it does not protect them either. What you do matters more than the kilometres.
Three things carry most of the weight:

ul: An end date or a real plan to close the distance. It does not need an exact day, but both people should be able to answer "When and where will we live together, and who moves?" Open-ended distance with no plan is the hardest kind.
Trust. You cannot see each other's days. Trust grows when people do what they say, share their lives without being asked, and do not need to be checked on.
A routine. Regular, predictable contact (for example, a short call most evenings and a longer video date at the weekend) makes the relationship feel stable without long hours online.

body.note: A plan you both agree on is more important than any texting rule. If one of you wants to close the distance and the other does not, that is the real conversation to have.

sections.h: Why talking well matters more than talking a lot
body: A diary study by Jiang and Hancock found that long-distance couples often felt as intimate as couples living nearby, or more so. Two things helped: sharing more personal thoughts and feelings, and seeing each other in a positive light. In other words, partners at a distance tend to make each conversation count.

This means you do not need to stay on a video call all day. Many couples feel worse when contact becomes a duty. What helps is quality: telling the other person what really happened today, how you felt, and asking about their life in detail.

The Gottman Institute describes small "bids for connection": a funny photo, a short message, a question. Responding to these bids, instead of ignoring them, builds trust over time. At a distance, bids happen mostly in chat apps, so answering them warmly matters even more.

sections.h: How often to talk and how to handle time zones
body: There is no correct number of calls. Agree on a rhythm that fits both of your lives and change it when life changes, such as during exams or a busy month at work.

head: Situation
A rhythm that often works
What to say
rows: Same time zone, busy jobs
Short messages during the day, one call most evenings
"Can we do a 20-minute call after dinner most days, and a longer one on Sunday?"
3 to 6 hours apart
A fixed overlap window (your morning, their evening)
"Your 9 p.m. is my 6 p.m. Can that be our usual call time?"
7 or more hours apart
Voice notes and messages to bridge the gap, two or three planned calls a week
"I'll send you a voice note before bed so you wake up to it."
One person has a heavy week
Lower contact for a set time, said clearly
"This week is crazy. I'll message less, but I'll call you on Friday."

body: Practical tips for time zones: keep both clocks on your phone, put the agreed call times in a shared calendar, and take turns being the one who stays up late or wakes up early. Fairness here prevents quiet resentment.
If a call has to be missed, say so before, not after. "I can't call tonight, I'm still at work. Tomorrow at 8?" is better than silence and an explanation the next day.
Shared activities give you something to talk about other than "How was your day?" Some ideas that work in most countries and on most apps:

ul: Watch the same film or series at the same time and talk during it on a call.
Cook the same recipe on a video call and eat together.
Play an online game together, or a simple board game over video.
Read the same book and talk about one chapter a week.
Take a walk while on a voice call and describe what you see.
Make a shared photo album or playlist and add to it every week.
Send a letter or a small parcel by post. Something physical from the other person feels very different from a message.
Plan your next visit together: places to go, food to try.
Study or work quietly on a video call, like sitting in the same room.

body: Visits are what keep the relationship real. Some tips that help:

ol: Always know when the next visit is. Having a date on the calendar makes hard weeks easier.
Share the cost and the travel fairly. If one person always travels or always pays, talk about it before it becomes a problem.
Do not try to fit everything into one visit. Leave time for ordinary things like grocery shopping and doing nothing. You are testing what daily life together would be like.
Meet each other's friends and, when it feels right, family. It helps you understand the other person's world.
Expect the goodbye to be hard, and expect a dip after it. Plan a call for the day after.

body: Some couples find the first days of a visit a little awkward after weeks apart. That is normal. It usually passes within a day.
At a distance, your mind fills the gaps. A late reply or a photo with a new friend can feel bigger than it is. Some ways to handle this:

ul: Say the feeling, not an accusation. Try "I felt a bit left out when I saw the party photos. Can you tell me about it?" instead of "Why didn't you tell me you were going out?"
Share your plans without being asked: "I'm going to dinner with people from work tonight, I'll message you when I'm home." This is not reporting, it is including the other person.
Do not ask for passwords, location tracking or proof of where they are. Checking does not build trust. If you feel you need to check, talk about why.
Notice your own pattern. Some people feel very anxious when replies are slow. cv.cm's attachment style test can help you see your own pattern and explain it to your partner.

body.note: Jealousy that turns into control is a warning sign: demanding to see your phone, telling you who you cannot see, or getting angry when you go out. See cv.cm's article on red flags in a relationship.

sections.h: Signs it is not working, and how to close the distance

head: Sign
What it may mean
What to do
rows: Calls feel like a duty for one or both of you
The routine no longer fits, or interest is fading
Change the rhythm and talk about how you each feel
There is no plan to live in the same place, and no one wants to make one
One person may not see a shared future
Ask directly: "Do you see us living together? When?"
Visits keep being cancelled
Low priority, money problems, or doubts
Ask what is getting in the way, and agree on the next date
You feel more anxious than happy most of the time
Your needs are not being met
Say what you need clearly. If nothing changes, it is okay to end it
One person lies about plans or new people
Broken trust
Talk honestly; repeated lying is a serious problem

body: Closing the distance is a big decision. Talk about where you will live, work or study, money, visas if needed, and how the person who moves will build a life there with their own friends and activities. Moving in after long distance is a new phase. Expect some adjustment as you learn each other's daily habits.
If you decide to end it, say so clearly and kindly, ideally on a video call rather than in a message. See cv.cm's article on how to break up with someone.

faq.a: Many do. Research has found that long-distance couples can feel as satisfied as couples who live close, but they break up at similar rates. A shared plan to close the distance and steady trust matter most.

faq.q: How often should you talk in a long-distance relationship?
faq.a: There is no fixed rule. Most couples do well with some daily contact and a few longer calls a week. Agree on a rhythm that feels good to both of you, and change it when life gets busy.

faq.q: How long can a long-distance relationship last without seeing each other?
faq.a: It depends on the couple, money and travel rules. What helps most is always knowing when the next visit is. Long periods with no plan to meet are hard for most people.

faq.q: Is it normal to fight more in a long-distance relationship?
faq.a: Small misunderstandings are common because messages lose tone. Move important or tense talks to a voice or video call, and say feelings rather than accusations.

faq.q: How do you keep the spark in a long-distance relationship?
faq.a: Do things together, not just talk about your day: watch a film at the same time, cook together on video, send letters, and plan visits. New shared experiences keep the relationship lively.
